766	\subsection{Extended Discussion}
767	\label{app:extended_discussion}
768	
769	\paragraph{Cross-strategy conditional decomposition.}
770	The two-stage pipeline (strategy identification followed by depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp over the na\"ive pooled classifier.
771	Under correct strategy routing, four-class accuracy reaches 72.6\% vs.\ 68.0\% under misrouting ($N{=}103{,}498$ / $76{,}502$), a gap of 4.6\,pp; d0 accuracy remains near-ceiling (${\sim}99.6$\%) regardless of routing, confirming that the d0 signal is strategy-invariant.
772	Even the worst routing yields a floor of 67.6\% ($2.7\times$ chance), and the 31.5\,pp d1--d3 gap between correct and wrong routing confirms feature-space misalignment rather than uniform noise.
773	End-to-end PLMs lag RF by ${\sim}20$\,pp, suggesting that current pretrained representations do not capture the distributional tail statistics that drive depth discrimination.
774	
775	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation (inconclusive preliminary evidence).}
776	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
777	Recursive generation depth estimation could enable a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) while down-weighting high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
778	A pilot study (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}) yields inconclusive evidence: the RF-vs-unfiltered comparison is not significant ($p>0.4$), though RF-filtered subsets outperform size-matched random subsampling ($p<0.001$--$0.02$ before Bonferroni correction; $p<0.003$--$0.06$ after correction at $\alpha{=}0.05/3{=}0.017$, with 2 of 3 comparisons surviving).
779	The d1/d2 boundary inversion under cross-strategy transfer further limits practical curation without strategy metadata.
780	Large-scale validation is needed before depth-graduated filtering can be considered practical.
781	
782	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
783	Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes.
784	Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
785	Source attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
786	Depth estimation characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
787	A layered provenance system combining these three signals (watermark presence, source model, and recursive generation depth) could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.
788	
789	\subsection{Computational Resources and Reproducibility}
790	\label{app:compute}
791	
792	\paragraph{Hardware.}
793	All experiments were conducted on 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (48\,GB) GPUs locally and 2$\times$ NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (48\,GB) on cloud instances.
794	Total computation is approximately 200 GPU$\cdot$hours, covering the $3 \times 3$ generation matrix (LoRA fine-tuning + sampling at each depth), feature extraction, depth extension to d5, 7--14B QLoRA experiments, and all ablations.
795	
796	\paragraph{Software.}
797	Key library versions: PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128, Transformers 5.8.1, PEFT 0.7.1, scikit-learn 1.8.0.
798	Additional dependencies: Accelerate 1.13.0, Datasets 4.8.4, XGBoost 3.2.0, NumPy 2.2.6 (Python 3.12.3, CUDA 12.8).
799	
800	\paragraph{Hyperparameters.}
801	LoRA hyperparameters ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, batch size 8, 3 epochs) follow \citet{hu2022lora}.
802	The Random Forest classifier uses 200 trees, Gini criterion, and no max depth, without hyperparameter search; all reported results use 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
803	
804	\paragraph{Inference cost.}
805	Feature extraction requires a single forward pass of the reference model.
806	On a single GPU this takes approximately 2 minutes for 5{,}000 passages; a CPU-only alternative requires approximately 50 minutes on server-grade hardware.
807	RF classification adds negligible overhead ($<$1\,s).

Now I'm moving through the review summary. The paper has clear strengths: the task formalization is novel and well-motivated, the benchmark is comprehensive at 180K samples with systematic design, the empirical analysis includes thorough ablations, and the authors are transparent about limitations. On the weaknesses side, the abstract is too dense with numbers and reads more like a results table, the discussion section is quite thin relative to the conclusion, and the methodological novelty is limited since it relies on standard approaches.

The practical constraints are significant—the work only explores full-replacement scenarios without accumulation experiments, which severely limits real-world applicability. Cross-strategy transfer performance is weak at 45.9% for the d1-d3 metric, which raises deployment concerns. There are also some stylistic issues suggesting AI-generated text, and while the EDD metric is novel, it's essentially a reformatted version of pairwise AUC reporting. The downstream curation proof-of-concept doesn't reach statistical significance.

Overall, this lands at a 3.0 for findings—the task and benchmark have genuine value and the evaluation is systematic, but the limited methodological innovation combined with the restriction to full-replacement settings and underdeveloped discussion section keeps it below conference threshold.

/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/docs/paper/generalization.tex:101:A two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp, with a 31.5\,pp d1--d3 gap between correct and wrong routing confirming feature-space misalignment (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}).

/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/docs/paper/section_appendix.tex:730:The top-2 features (\texttt{p90\_ppl} + \texttt{var\_surprisal}) retain combined importance of 28.7\%, confirming that perplexity tail statistics remain the dominant depth markers even after augmentation.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/docs/paper/section_appendix.tex:771:Under correct strategy routing, four-class accuracy reaches 72.6\% vs.\ 68.0\% under misrouting ($N{=}103{,}498$ / $76{,}502$), a gap of 4.6\,pp; d0 accuracy remains near-ceiling (${\sim}99.6$\%) regardless of routing, confirming that the d0 signal is strategy-invariant.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0513_2/projects/recursive_gen_depth_est/docs/paper/section_appendix.tex:773:End-to-end PLMs lag RF by ${\sim}20$\,pp, suggesting that current pretrained representations do not capture the distributional tail statistics that drive depth discrimination.

## Recursive Training & Synthetic Data in LLMs

Recursive Language Models (RLMs) show performance advantages depending on data type: RLMs outperform traditional LLMs on synthetic data with labels, perform worse on synthetic Oolong data, but significantly outperform LLMs on real data, demonstrating the value of sub-LLM reliance for complex data.

Research demonstrates that model collapse cannot be avoided when training solely on synthetic data, but when mixing real and synthetic data, there's an estimate of a maximal amount of synthetic data below which model collapse can be avoided.

Recent 2025 research includes studies on "Strong Model Collapse" (ICLR 2025), "Towards a Theoretical Understanding of Synthetic Data in LLM Post-Training" (ICLR 2025), and "Beyond Model Collapse: Scaling Up with Synthesized Data Requires Reinforcement" (ICLR 2025).

## Synthetic Data in 2026

High-quality human training data is scarce and expensive to collect, particularly for rare edge cases, which is why synthetic data generation mixed with curated human data is becoming increasingly important. Without new training fuel, model performance on real-world use cases risks model collapse where models remix their own past outputs, making high-quality human data critical.
